passages.title: Waiting for the perfect picture
passages.text:
Wildlife photographer Emma Hartley talks about her work.

People often imagine that my job involves travelling to beautiful places and taking amazing pictures every day. The truth is rather different. I spend most of my time waiting – sometimes for days – and on many trips I come home without a single photo I'm happy with.

I became interested in wildlife when I was about ten. My grandfather lent me his old camera, and I used to sit in his garden trying to photograph the birds at the feeder. Most of the pictures were terrible, but I loved the challenge of staying still and quiet for so long. I didn't think of photography as a career, though. At university I studied biology, and I planned to become a scientist.

Everything changed during my final year, when I joined a research trip to Scotland to count sea birds. I took my camera along just for fun, but one of the scientists saw my photos and sent them to a nature magazine. To my surprise, they printed three of them. That was when I realised that I could combine my two interests.

The first few years weren't easy. I earned very little and had to work in a camera shop at weekends to pay the rent. But the job taught me a lot about equipment, and I met photographers who gave me useful advice.

Nowadays I work mainly for magazines and conservation organisations. Before a trip, I spend weeks reading about the animal I want to photograph: where it feeds, when it is most active and how it reacts to people. Good preparation matters far more than an expensive camera. Last spring, for example, I wanted to photograph otters in Norway. Local fishermen told me the otters came out at dawn, so I was in my hiding place by four o'clock every morning. On the sixth day, a mother and two young otters appeared just metres away.

The part of the job I find hardest is not the cold or the early mornings but being away from my family. My son is seven now, and I try not to accept jobs that last more than two weeks.

Young people often ask me how to start. My answer is always the same: begin close to home. You don't need to travel to Africa. A local park is full of wildlife if you are patient enough to look for it. And remember that the animal always comes first. If it seems stressed, put your camera down and walk away. No photo is worth frightening an animal.

questions.question: What does Emma say about her job in the first paragraph?
options: a) It is as exciting as most people think.
b) It is easy to get good photos on most trips.
c) She usually knows exactly when the animals will appear.
d) Most of her time is spent waiting.
questions.explanation: Emma says 'I spend most of my time waiting – sometimes for days'. She says 'the truth is rather different' from what people imagine, so it is not as exciting as people think, and 'on many trips I come home without a single photo I'm happy with', so good photos are not easy to get.

questions.question: What did Emma enjoy about photographing birds as a child?
options: a) Seeing how good her photos were.
b) Learning the names of different garden birds.
c) Having to be patient and silent for a long time.
d) Showing her pictures to her grandfather in his garden.
questions.explanation: She says 'I loved the challenge of staying still and quiet for so long'. Her photos were not good ('Most of the pictures were terrible'), and the text does not mention showing them to her grandfather or learning bird names.

questions.question: How did Emma's career as a photographer begin?
options: a) A scientist sent some of her photos to a magazine.
b) She went to Scotland to take photos for a magazine.
c) Her university teachers told her to study photography.
d) A magazine offered her a job when she finished university.
questions.explanation: On the research trip 'one of the scientists saw my photos and sent them to a nature magazine', which printed three of them. She went to Scotland 'to count sea birds', not to work for a magazine, and she took her camera 'just for fun'.

questions.question: What does Emma think about preparing for a trip?
options: a) Knowing about the animal is more important than having good equipment.
b) She must ask local fishermen for advice before every trip.
c) She needs to buy a more expensive camera for each new animal.
d) She should never plan to stay in one place for more than six days.
questions.explanation: She reads about where the animal feeds and when it is active, and says 'Good preparation matters far more than an expensive camera.' The fishermen in Norway are only one example, and seeing the otters 'on the sixth day' does not mean she limits her trips to six days.

questions.question: What advice would Emma give to a young person who wants to photograph wildlife?
options: a) "Buy the best camera you can afford before you start."
b) "Practise near where you live, and never upset the animals."
c) "Get as close as you can to an animal, even if it seems nervous."
d) "Save up so that you can travel to places like Africa."
questions.explanation: Emma tells young people to 'begin close to home' because 'a local park is full of wildlife', and says 'If it seems stressed, put your camera down and walk away. No photo is worth frightening an animal.' She says 'You don't need to travel to Africa', and earlier that an expensive camera matters less than preparation.
